content_preview.title: Cursor, GitHub and Anthropic Each Describe New Source-Control Infrastructure for Agent-Driven Change Volume, While Zed Adds a Thread Layer Above Git
content_preview.summary: Between August and October 2026, Cursor, GitHub and Anthropic described repository infrastructure designed around agent load; they differ on whether to keep Git, and the performance figures are self-reported.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Background

Git is built as a decentralized system. In Anthropic's description, [every clone is a complete, self-contained repository](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/redesigning-source-control) that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while offline, and Anthropic says this is the right design for the vast majority of repositories. Hosting platforms nonetheless run Git as a centralized service. [GitHub's engineering blog](https://github.blog/engineering...

editor_notes.content_quality: A genuine multi-development Analysis: four public accounts (Cursor Continuity/Origin, GitHub's Spokes-to-blob-storage redesign, Anthropic's Scion, Zed Delta) compared on where authoritative state lives, whether Git stays, how merge queues are treated, and how far the lessons travel. Reported facts (Current situation) are separated from the Herald's comparison (Implications), which is explicitly labelled as drawn from the sources and not a prediction. No opinion or forecast in the Herald's voice; Anthropic's six-to-12-month expectation is attributed to Anthropic. Body is 1,429 words with link URLs stripped (script count 1429; range 800-2000). Title is exactly 148 characters (cap 150). Analysis requirements met: examines a topic rather than one release.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 9 snapshots (source-0..8.html.gz, HTTP 200, no archive fallback, no suspicious_patterns) read from disk. Allowlist hosts verified by exact hostname: github.blog, thenewstack.io, anthropic.com, infoq.com, theregister.com are all present in config/source_allowlist.txt; no edits needed. source-0 (GitHub blog, Oct 6 2026, updated Oct 26): confirms Spokes keeps a full copy on several fileservers, five by default; three-phase commit with quorum; 'adding replicas to absorb read load makes writes slower'; pushes 4.9x (0.69B to 3.35B per month); PR merges nearly 4x; Actions 3.26B runs in September; 'Merges contend on one reference' wording; 'Authoritative repository data lives in Azure Blob Storage'; 'Build on the workflows developers already trust... same workflows at much higher volumes'; 'driving the next architectural shift'. The 'In internal benchmarks, it has delivered up to 35 times higher write throughput' sentence is verbatim in the GitHub post (my first keyword search for '35x' missed it; found on re-search for 'benchmark'); The Register separately describes 35x as an expectation, so the article's attribution to GitHub's internal benchmarks is correct. source-4 (Anthropic): confirms 'every clone is a complete, self-contained repository', 'vast majority of repositories', 2,500 -> 30,000 per day, ~100 GB history, 25M checkouts/day, several hundred Git mirrors at peak, 200x smaller footprint, two orders of magnitude faster checkouts, Mononoke footnote, 'by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use', 'six to 12 months', the tokens statement, and the merge-queue passage ('We haven't been able to effectively replicate the industry standard of a global repository lock on the merge queue... post-merge and pre-deploy automated testing... Claude can typically fix these conflicts faster than humans can even identify them'). source-5 (InfoQ, Oct 27): quoted caveat 'company-reported results for its internal workload, not general benchmarks against Git' verbatim; 'Scion depends on server availability, and the required integration is substantial'; 'reconsider where work happens'. source-1 (New Stack, Scion): 'wants to partner with GitHub, GitLab and the open source community', 'fully migrated its monorepo ... in just five months', no public release. source-2 (New Stack, GitHub): 'Now, GitHub says it has added 4 million CPU cores, plus 160 petabytes ... so far this year'; 2.9B commits/month in August up from 1.4B in April; Parikh quote 'Agents are changing the volume and shape of software development' verbatim. source-6 (Register, Oct 28): 7.4B commits in September 2026, five times a year earlier; ~84% 90-day availability low on May 7 from reconstructed status-page data; 'Those commitments have put four million CPU cores and 160 petabytes of high-speed storage on its infrastructure roadmap'; Parikh 'We expect to complete the migration early next year'. The Register ('on its infrastructure roadmap') and The New Stack ('has added ... so far this year') genuinely differ on the four-million-core figure; the article reports both wordings without choosing. source-7 (Register, Aug 23): Martí post, Origin powered by Continuity, WAL in S3, local reference copy, 'More code, more PRs, more CI runs' verbatim, 'We will see how well this approach plays out as Origin moves into being a production service'. source-8 (Register, Oct 13): Piper, VFS for Git, Sapling named; no open source release; 25M checkouts. source-3 (New Stack, Zed, Sep 16): public beta; 'Delta currently works with Git repositories'; DeltaDB adds a layer between commits; 33 developers, 570 changes to main; Sobo quotes ('GitHub has an established social component that will take longer to replace', 'moving more thoughtfully', hundreds of monthly contributors) verbatim and from an interview ('tells The New Stack'); Cursor launched Origin in August; GitLab Project Switch in private beta. Minor note: The Register's Cursor piece says Spokes keeps 'at least three' copies while GitHub's post says five by default; the article correctly uses GitHub's own figure. INDEPENDENT-SOURCE COUNT (strict): 3 independent outlets (The Register x3, The New Stack x3, InfoQ x1, 7 articles) plus 2 first-party sources (Anthropic, GitHub, cited for primary facts only). Whether the outlets add more than the vendors' claims: partly. The New Stack's Zed piece is based on an interview with Sobo and adds the market context (Origin, Project Switch); The Register's GitHub piece adds reconstructed status-page availability data and outage chronology and independently reports the 'roadmap' wording; The Register's Scion piece adds comparison to Piper/VFS/Sapling; The Register's Cursor piece adds commentary and GitHub context; InfoQ adds an architect-oriented assessment and the explicit 'not general benchmarks' caveat. The Scion and Cursor coverage is otherwise largely relayed vendor material (the article itself says the outlets 'largely relay and contextualise'). None reproduced benchmarks. The policy criterion is independence from the subject (not the vendor's own pages); it is clearly met by at least 2 outlets (3 here), the evidence is modest on performance claims, and the article states that limit in Background and 'What remains unknown'. Judgment: requirement met, but with the limit disclosed; approved on that basis. Cursor has no primary source cited: its architecture is known only through The Register's account of a Martí post (see correction 2).
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All figures are attributed to GitHub, Anthropic, Cursor or the reporting outlet, with dates. Checked: 7.4B commits (Register; GitHub's own post says 7.38B), 2.9B/1.4B (New Stack), 4.9x pushes, 3.26B Actions, 2,500/30,000 merges per day, 200x footprint, 570 changes by 33 developers. The GitHub '35 times higher write throughput' claim is correctly attributed to GitHub's internal benchmarks (verbatim in source-0). Cursor Origin was launched in August (Register, New Stack); the article's internal links resolve to real files: 2026-08/28 Continuity, 2026-08/19 Origin launch (correctly dated August, not misdated), 2026-09/18 Zed Delta launch. Orphan-link diff: every body URL is in sources and vice versa (empty set difference both ways). Implications are labelled as comparison, not prediction; the 'where authoritative state lives' statements each trace to The Register (Cursor), GitHub and Anthropic. 'Each describe' in the title: GitHub and Anthropic do so in first-party posts; Cursor's is known via The Register's report of Martí's post only.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and attributed. Anthropic's claims are consistently framed as the company's own ('Anthropic says', 'Anthropic reports') and InfoQ's 'company-reported' caveat is quoted verbatim. No promotional language, no AI self-reference.
editor_notes.originality: New. No existing Herald article covers Scion or the Oct 6 GitHub Git-infrastructure post; Continuity, Origin and Zed Delta were covered as news earlier and are linked for continuity, not repeated. This article's angle is the cross-vendor comparison.
concerns: Conflict of interest: Anthropic is a central subject (Scion, its monorepo and merge queue) and makes the Claude models used by this newsroom's writer and reviewer. The article does not disclose this. All Anthropic statements are attributed to Anthropic, The Register, InfoQ or The New Stack and read neutrally; a reader-facing clarification is filed (correction 1), consistent with the Bun and watermark/API-controls Analyses.
Cursor's account rests solely on The Register's report of a Cursor engineer's post; there is no Cursor primary source in the source set. Filed as a clarification (correction 2).
Independent outlets add context and some original data (status-page reconstruction, a Sobo interview) but little independent verification of performance claims; the article discloses this.
recommendations: For future infrastructure comparisons, cite each vendor's primary post (including Cursor's) and take care to distinguish measured benchmarks from stated expectations.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Substantively sound Analysis that satisfies the policy requirements (9 sources, 3 independent outlets, topic-level examination, facts separated from analysis, 1,429 words, 148-character title). Approved with two clarifications: the undisclosed Anthropic relationship and Cursor's second-hand sourcing. Featured candidacy: 2 - significant for a broad developer audience, covering how three major vendors rebuild source-control infrastructure under agent load and where they diverge on Git
